context.text: The question had been rising since the Holy Ghost fell on the household of Cornelius, a Roman centurion at Caesarea, while Peter was still speaking, and Peter had them baptized. At Antioch men of Cyprus and Cyrene preached to the Grecians and a great number believed, and there "the disciples were called Christians first". Barnabas and Paul, sent out from Antioch, came back from their first journey and told the church how God "had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles".

Then "certain men which came down from Judaea taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved." Paul and Barnabas had "no small dissension and disputation with them", and the church of Antioch sent them up to Jerusalem "unto the apostles and elders about this question". There some believers of the party of the Pharisees held that the Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.

narrative.text: The apostles and elders came together to consider the matter, and there was "much disputing". Peter rose and reminded them that God had chosen him to bring the Gospel to the Gentiles, and had given them the Holy Ghost "even as he did unto us", making no difference between them. Why then lay on the disciples a yoke "which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear"? "But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they."

The whole assembly kept silence while Barnabas and Paul told of the miracles and wonders God had worked among the Gentiles through them. Then James spoke, the brother of the Lord, whom Eusebius records as the first bishop of the church of Jerusalem. He showed from the prophets that God had long purposed to call the nations, and gave his judgment:

Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God: But that we write unto them, that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood.

The apostles and elders, "with the whole church", chose Judas Barsabas and Silas to go to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They carried a letter to the Gentile believers of Antioch, Syria and Cilicia, which disowned those who had troubled them, "to whom we gave no such commandment", and set down what the assembly had decided:

For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things; That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well.

At Antioch the letter was read to the gathered church, and "they rejoiced for the consolation"; Judas and Silas, prophets themselves, strengthened the brethren with many words. In his letter to the Galatians Paul tells of a visit to Jerusalem, often taken to be this one, on which Titus, a Greek who came with him, was not compelled to be circumcised, and "James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars" gave him and Barnabas "the right hands of fellowship".

significance.text: The Church has read this meeting as the first of her councils and the pattern of those that followed: the apostles and elders gathered, heard one another, tested the new demand against the Scriptures and against what God had done, and answered with one letter. The fifth Ecumenical Council, at Constantinople in 553, recalled it as its own example:

For although the grace of the Holy Spirit abounded in each one of the Apostles, so that no one of them needed the counsel of another in the execution of his work, yet they were not willing to define on the question then raised touching the circumcision of the Gentiles, until being gathered together they had confirmed their own several sayings by the testimony of the divine Scriptures.
significance.source: The Sentence of the Second Council of Constantinople (553), tr. H. R. Percival (NPNF2 vol. 14, 1900)

significance.text: The letter's words, "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us", join the judgment of the assembly to the Holy Spirit; St John Chrysostom comments that "it is not man's doing". He also saw in the order of the meeting, each heard in turn and James speaking last, a lesson in humility: "There was no arrogance in the Church." The decision kept the Gospel open to every nation without asking the nations first to keep the Law of Moses.

consequences.text: Paul and Silas carried the decision into Asia Minor: in city after city "they delivered them the decrees for to keep, that were ordained of the apostles and elders which were at Jerusalem", and the churches were established in the faith. Paul's letter to the Galatians shows how hard the question remained: at Antioch Peter drew back from eating with Gentiles when men came from James, and Paul "withstood him to the face".

uncertainty: Acts gives no year. The council is usually placed about 49, reckoning from Paul's letters, among them the "fourteen years" of Galatians 2:1, and from the order of events in Acts; the exact year cannot be fixed. Whether the visit Paul describes in Galatians 2 is this one or the earlier famine visit of Acts 11:30 is disputed, and with it whether Peter's withdrawal at Antioch came before or after the council. Acts does not call this James the brother of the Lord, but James the son of Zebedee had already been killed (Acts 12:2), and Paul names "James the Lord's brother" at Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19); Eusebius and Chrysostom both call him its bishop.

people.name: St Peter the Apostle
people.role: Reminded the assembly that God gave the Spirit to the Gentiles of Cornelius's house, and spoke against laying the Law on them.

people.name: St James, the Brother of the Lord
people.role: Leader of the church at Jerusalem, recorded as its first bishop; spoke last and gave the judgment the letter carried.

people.name: St Paul the Apostle
people.role: With Barnabas brought the question from Antioch and told of God's work among the Gentiles; Galatians gives his own account.

people.name: St Barnabas
people.role: Paul's companion on the first journey and at Jerusalem; returned with the letter to Antioch.

people.name: St Silas
people.role: A leading man of the Jerusalem church and a prophet, chosen with Judas Barsabas to carry the letter; then Paul's companion.

people.name: St Titus
people.role: Paul's Greek companion on the visit told in Galatians 2, who was not compelled to be circumcised.

people.name: St John the Apostle
people.role: One of the "pillars" at Jerusalem who, with James and Peter, gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship.

review.basis: Rests on Acts 10-16 and Galatians 1-2 (King James Version), with the Sentence of the council of 553 (Percival, NPNF2 vol. 14), Chrysostom's homilies on Acts and Eusebius's Church History in their NPNF translations. Quotations are verbatim; the rest is our paraphrase of Acts.
